claim: Dispatched is an essential component of the machinery that deploys Hedgehog family ligands from producing cells.
source: The transmembrane protein Dispatched is an essential component of the machinery that deploys Hedgehog family ligands from producing cells, and is absolutely required for signaling to long-range targets.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about Dispatched function.

claim: Dispatched is absolutely required for signaling to long-range targets.
source: The transmembrane protein Dispatched is an essential component of the machinery that deploys Hedgehog family ligands from producing cells, and is absolutely required for signaling to long-range targets.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about Dispatched function.

claim: Vertebrate Dispatched is activated by proprotein convertase-mediated cleavage at a conserved processing site in its first extracellular loop.
source: Herein, we reveal vertebrate Dispatched is activated by proprotein convertase-mediated cleavage at a conserved processing site in its first extracellular loop.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study presented in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Dispatched processing occurs at the cell surface.
source: Dispatched processing occurs at the cell surface to instruct its membrane re-localization in polarized epithelial cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cell surface biotinylation experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Dispatched processing instructs its membrane re-localization in polarized epithelial cells.
source: Dispatched processing occurs at the cell surface to instruct its membrane re-localization in polarized epithelial cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by localization studies in Drosophila follicle cells shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: Cleavage site mutation alters Dispatched membrane trafficking.
source: Cleavage site mutation alters Dispatched membrane trafficking and reduces ligand release, leading to compromised pathway activity in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing altered localization in follicle cells (Figure 6D) and reduced Rab5 colocalization (Figure 6F-G).

claim: Cleavage site mutation reduces ligand release.
source: Cleavage site mutation alters Dispatched membrane trafficking and reduces ligand release, leading to compromised pathway activity in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Shh release assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cleavage site mutation leads to compromised pathway activity in vivo.
source: Cleavage site mutation alters Dispatched membrane trafficking and reduces ligand release, leading to compromised pathway activity in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by reporter assays (Figure 4A) and Drosophila wing phenotypes (Figure 5D-F).

claim: Convertase-mediated cleavage is required for Dispatched maturation and functional competency in Hedgehog ligand-producing cells.
source: As such, convertase-mediated cleavage is required for Dispatched maturation and functional competency in Hedgehog ligand-producing cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: Hedgehog ligands are produced as precursor proteins that undergo autocatalytic processing.
source: Hedgehog (Hh) ligands are produced as precursor proteins that undergo autocatalytic processing whereby a carboxyl-terminal intein-like domain cleaves itself, in a cholesterol-dependent manner, from an amino-terminal signaling domain (Guy, 2000; Lee et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: The Hedgehog signaling protein is covalently modified by cholesterol on its carboxyl-terminal cysteine.
source: The resulting ~20 kDa signaling protein is covalently modified by cholesterol on its new carboxyl-terminal cysteine and by a long chain fatty acid on its amino-terminus (Porter et al., 1996a; Chamoun et al., 2001; Pepinsky et al., 1998; Long et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: The Hedgehog signaling protein is covalently modified by a long chain fatty acid on its amino-terminus.
source: The resulting ~20 kDa signaling protein is covalently modified by cholesterol on its new carboxyl-terminal cysteine and by a long chain fatty acid on its amino-terminus (Porter et al., 1996a; Chamoun et al., 2001; Pepinsky et al., 1998; Long et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Shh lipid modifications contribute to physiological Sonic Hh activity by governing ligand distribution across developing tissues.
source: These lipid modifications contribute to physiological Sonic Hh (Shh) activity by governing ligand distribution across developing tissues, and influencing ligand potency toward target cells (Long et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2001; Li et al., 2006; Porter et al., 1996b; Burke et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Shh lipid modifications influence ligand potency toward target cells.
source: These lipid modifications contribute to physiological Sonic Hh (Shh) activity by governing ligand distribution across developing tissues, and influencing ligand potency toward target cells (Long et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2001; Li et al., 2006; Porter et al., 1996b; Burke et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Shh lipid modifications confer high membrane affinity to the mature ligand, thereby anchoring it to the producing cell surface.
source: Distribution is controlled by Shh lipid modifications conferring high membrane affinity to the mature ligand, thereby anchoring it to the producing cell surface.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Shh must be deployed from producing cell membranes through a process that is dependent upon Dispatched 1 (Disp).
source: In order to reach long-range target cells, Shh must be deployed from producing cell membranes through a process that is dependent upon Dispatched 1 (Disp), a predicted twelve-pass transmembrane protein that shares homology with the bacterial Resistance, Nodulation and Division (RND) Transporter superfamily (Burke et al., 1999; Caspary et al., 2002; Ma et al., 2002; Kawakami et al., 2002; Amanai and Jiang, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Dispatched 1 is a predicted twelve-pass transmembrane protein.
source: In order to reach long-range target cells, Shh must be deployed from producing cell membranes through a process that is dependent upon Dispatched 1 (Disp), a predicted twelve-pass transmembrane protein that shares homology with the bacterial Resistance, Nodulation and Division (RND) Transporter superfamily (Burke et al., 1999; Caspary et al., 2002; Ma et al., 2002; Kawakami et al., 2002; Amanai and Jiang, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Dispatched 1 shares homology with the bacterial Resistance, Nodulation and Division (RND) Transporter superfamily.
source: In order to reach long-range target cells, Shh must be deployed from producing cell membranes through a process that is dependent upon Dispatched 1 (Disp), a predicted twelve-pass transmembrane protein that shares homology with the bacterial Resistance, Nodulation and Division (RND) Transporter superfamily (Burke et al., 1999; Caspary et al., 2002; Ma et al., 2002; Kawakami et al., 2002; Amanai and Jiang, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Disp1 knockout mice phenocopy animals lacking the essential Shh signal transducing component Smoothened (Smo).
source: Disp1 knockout mice phenocopy animals lacking the essential Shh signal transducing component Smoothened (Smo), underscoring the importance of Disp for pathway activity during early development (Caspary et al., 2002; Ma et al., 2002; Kawakami et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: In vertebrates, Disp functions with the secreted glycoprotein Scube2 to facilitate Shh membrane extraction.
source: In vertebrates, Disp functions with the secreted glycoprotein Scube2 to facilitate Shh membrane extraction (Ma et al., 2002; Creanga et al., 2012; Tukachinsky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Disp contains a sterol sensing domain (SSD) that is thought to interact with the Shh cholesterol modification.
source: However, Disp contains a sterol sensing domain (SSD) that is thought to interact with the Shh cholesterol modification to position the ligand for transfer to Scube2 (Creanga et al., 2012; Tukachinsky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Disp must organize into trimers to release Shh.
source: Biochemical and cell biological analyses have shown Disp must organize into trimers and localize to the basolateral cell surface to release Shh (Etheridge et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Disp must localize to the basolateral cell surface to release Shh.
source: Biochemical and cell biological analyses have shown Disp must organize into trimers and localize to the basolateral cell surface to release Shh (Etheridge et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Apically localized Hh must be internalized in a Disp-dependent manner in Drosophila.
source: Genetic studies in Drosophila suggest a crucial role for Disp-mediated endosomal recycling during Hh deployment, demonstrating that apically localized Hh must be internalized in a Disp-dependent manner, and then retargeted to the cell surface to exit ligand-producing cells (D'Angelo et al., 2015; Callejo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Loss of Disp function triggers apical accumulation of Hh and disruption of long-range signaling.
source: Loss of Disp function triggers apical accumulation of Hh and disruption of long-range signaling (D'Angelo et al., 2015; Callejo et al., 2011), suggesting the ability of Disp to appropriately traffic with Hh is imperative for ligand release.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Western blot of cell lysates from NIH3T3 cells transfected with plasmid encoding DispHA revealed two distinct protein bands, one running near 175 kDa and a second with an apparent molecular weight of ~145 kDa.
source: Western blot of cell lysates from NIH3T3 cells transfected with plasmid encoding DispHA revealed two distinct protein bands detected by anti-HA antibody, one running near the predicted molecular weight of 175 kDa, hereafter referred to as Disp175, and a second with an apparent molecular weight of ~145 kDa, Disp145 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the western blot experiment shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Treatment with Endo H resolved a Disp protein species from Disp175, indicating a fraction of the upper band was ER-localized.
source: Treatment with Endo H, which removes simple N-glycans added in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), resolved a Disp protein species from Disp175, indicating a fraction of the upper band was ER-localized (Figure 1B lane 2, arrowhead).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Endo H treatment result shown in Figure 1B, based on the known specificity of Endo H for ER-localized glycans.

claim: The Disp145 band was resistant to Endo H.
source: The lower band was resistant to Endo H.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the western blot experiment shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PNGase F treatment significantly altered migration of Disp145, indicating post-ER localization of the smaller protein species.
source: However, PNGase F, which strips both simple and complex post-ER glycans, significantly altered migration of Disp145, indicating post-ER localization of the smaller protein species (lane 3, arrow).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PNGase F treatment result shown in Figure 1B, based on the known specificity of PNGase F for both ER and post-ER glycans.

claim: Disp175 is cleaved to generate a truncated protein after ER exit.
source: The observation that the Disp145 fraction was highly enriched for EndoH-resistant glycosylation, suggested Disp175 might be cleaved to generate a truncated protein after ER exit.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the glycosylation analysis data from Figure 1B.

claim: Disp175 was detected by both HA and V5 antisera.
source: Disp175 was detected by both HA and V5 antisera (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the western blot experiment shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Disp145 was detected only by HA, suggesting loss of the V5 epitope from the Disp145 species.
source: Conversely, Disp145 was detected only by HA, suggesting loss of the V5 epitope from the Disp145 species.
evidence: This is an observation from the western blot experiment shown in Figure 1C, with an inference about epitope loss.

claim: A ~ 30 kDa fragment was detected by V5 antisera, confirming that Disp protein is clipped to produce Disp145.
source: Accordingly, a ~ 30 kDa fragment was detected by V5 antisera, confirming that Disp protein is clipped to produce Disp145.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the western blot experiment shown in Figure 1C, with an inference about cleavage.

claim: Unprocessed Disp175 enriched in the non-biotinylated intracellular fraction.
source: Combined densitometry analysis of four independent experiments revealed that unprocessed Disp175 enriched in the non-biotinylated intracellular fraction. Approximately 60% of total Disp175 signal was detected in the unlabeled intracellular fraction with ~40% present on the cell surface (Figure 1D. lane 4 vs. 6, arrowhead and densitometry summary, purple).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the cell surface biotinylation experiment shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The processed 30 kDa V5Disp fragment was significantly enriched on the cell surface, accounting for ~76% of the total V5Disp30 signal.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the processed 30 kDa V5Disp fragment was significantly enriched on the cell surface, accounting for ~76% of the total V5Disp30 signal (Figure 4D, arrow and densitometry summary, green).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the cell surface biotinylation experiment shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Disp145 is likely generated from Disp175 at the cell surface.
source: Combined with the above deglycosylation analysis, these results suggest Disp145 is likely generated from Disp175 at the cell surface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biotinylation and glycosylation data from Figure 1.

claim: EVDWNF was identified as the amino-terminal sequence of Disp145, mapping to amino acids 280–285 in EC1 of the murine protein.
source: EVDWNF, which maps to amino acids 280–285 in EC1 of the murine protein, was identified as the amino-terminal sequence (Figure 2B, red line).
evidence: This is a direct result from Edman degradation sequencing shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The amino-terminal sequence of Disp145 is directly adjacent to a dibasic amino acid proprotein convertase (PC) cleavage motif that is conserved in Disp proteins from Drosophila, zebrafish, chick, mouse and human.
source: This is directly adjacent to a dibasic amino acid proprotein convertase (PC) cleavage motif that is conserved in Disp proteins from Drosophila, zebrafish, chick, mouse and human (Figure 2B, yellow box) (Seidah et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from the sequence alignment shown in Figure 2B, combined with knowledge about PC cleavage motifs.

claim: Disruption of the murine Disp convertase motif by R279A, E280A mutation (DispCS) appreciably reduced Disp175 to Disp145 conversion.
source: Consistent with this being a functional cleavage site, disruption of the murine Disp convertase motif by R279A, E280A mutation (DispCS) appreciably reduced Disp175 to Disp145 conversion, evidenced by nearly undetectable Disp145 or Disp 30 signal in DispCS cell lysates (Figure 2C, lane 3 and 2D, lane 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the western blot experiments shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The 175 kDa fraction of DispCS was predominantly Endo H resistant, indicating that failure to cleave was not likely due to the mutant protein being retained in the ER.
source: The 175 kDa fraction of DispCS was predominantly Endo H resistant, indicating that failure to cleave was not likely due to the mutant protein being retained in the ER (Figure 2C, lane 8).
evidence: This is an observation from the deglycosylation experiment shown in Figure 2C, with an inference about ER retention.

claim: CS mutation resulted in pronounced accumulation of a large molecular weight band (~250 kDa).
source: Notably, CS mutation resulted in pronounced accumulation of a large molecular weight band (~250 kDa) that was also evident for the wild-type protein, albeit at reduced intensity (Figure 2C lane 3 compared to 2, bracket).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the western blot experiment shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The 250 kDa fraction of DispCS was largely resistant to deglycosylating enzymes.
source: The 250 kDa fraction of DispCS was largely resistant to deglycosylating enzymes, suggesting the molecular weight shift was not due to alteration of N-glycosylation status (Figure 2C, lanes 7–9).
evidence: This is an observation from the deglycosylation experiment shown in Figure 2C, with an inference about glycosylation.

claim: Disp250 accumulated for both wild type and CS DispHA proteins at equal intensities following proteasome inhibition by MG132 treatment.
source: Moreover, Disp250 accumulated for both wild type and CS DispHA proteins at equal intensities following proteasome inhibition by MG132 treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the MG132 treatment experiment shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Treatment with increasing concentrations of Furin Inhibitor I dose-dependently reduced Disp145 levels.
source: Treatment with increasing concentrations of drug dose-dependently reduced Disp145 levels (Figure 3A, and green in bottom panel).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the Furin Inhibitor I treatment experiment shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Chemical inhibition of Furin family proteases triggered accumulation of the ~250 kDa fraction.
source: Instead, as was observed following mutation of the cleavage site (Figure 2C), chemical inhibition of Furin family proteases triggered accumulation of the ~250 kDa fraction (Figure 3A, bracket, and bottom panel, black).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the Furin Inhibitor I treatment experiment shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Knockout of Furin blocked formation of V5Disp30.
source: Knockout of Furin, which targets substrates in the trans-Golgi, at the cell surface and in recycling endosomes (Seidah et al., 2013), blocked formation of V5Disp30.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the CRISPR/Cas9 knockout experiment shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Knockout of PCSK5, PACE4 and PCSK7 did not block formation of V5Disp30.
source: Knockout of PCSK5, PACE4 and PCSK7 did not, identifying Furin as the candidate convertase responsible for Disp cleavage.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the CRISPR/Cas9 knockout experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Over-expression of epitope-tagged Furin-Myc with V5DispHA enhanced cleavage of the wild-type protein.
source: Accordingly, over-expression of epitope-tagged Furin-Myc with V5DispHA enhanced cleavage of the wild-type protein, and induced low-level cleavage of the CS mutant, suggesting that by increasing Furin protein levels compensatory and/or off-site cleavage can occur (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the Furin overexpression experiment shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both wild-type and CS mutant V5DispHA proteins were detected in anti-Myc immunoprecipitates, consistent with an interaction occurring between Furin and Disp.
source: Both wild-type and CS mutant V5DispHA proteins were detected in anti-Myc immunoprecipitates, consistent with an interaction occurring between Furin and Disp (right panel, lanes 5 and 7).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the co-immunoprecipitation experiment shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Murine V5DispHA protein expressed in LoVo cells failed to produce V5Disp30.
source: Conversely, murine V5DispHA protein expressed in LoVo cells failed to produce V5Disp30, and instead migrated in a manner similar to the CS mutant (lanes 2–3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the LoVo cell expression experiment shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Re-expression of Furin in LoVo cells rescued V5Disp30 production.
source: Cleavage disruption was specific to Furin loss because its re-expression in LoVo cells rescued V5Disp30 production (lane 4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the Furin rescue experiment in LoVo cells shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Co-culture of LightII cells with Disp-/- MEFs expressing GFP +Shh failed to induce a significant change in reporter gene activity over that of the GFP control.
source: Co-culture of LightII cells with Disp-/- MEFs expressing GFP +Shh failed to induce a significant change in reporter gene activity over that of the GFP control.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the reporter assay shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Co-culture of reporter cells with Shh-expressing MEFs transiently expressing wild-type DispHA induced a statistically significant reporter response.
source: Conversely, co-culture of reporter cells with Shh-expressing MEFs transiently expressing wild-type DispHA induced a statistically significant reporter response, consistent with Shh deployment being rescued by re-expression of wild-type DispHA protein.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the reporter assay shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Expression of DispCSHA in Shh-expressing Disp-/- MEFs affected LightII cell reporter activity similarly to the GFP control.
source: Expression of DispCSHA in Shh-expressing Disp-/- MEFs affected LightII cell reporter activity similarly to the GFP control.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the reporter assay shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Co-expression of Scube2-Flag with DispHA prompted a dose-dependent increase in Shh protein detectable in conditioned culture media.
source: Consistent with Scube2 partnering with Disp to facilitate ligand extraction from the membrane, co-expression of increasing levels of Scube2-Flag with DispHA prompted a dose-dependent increase in Shh protein detectable in conditioned culture media (lanes 8–10 and dark gray).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the Shh release assay shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cleavage-deficient DispCS failed to effectively promote Shh release into conditioned media when expressed alone or in combination with Scube2-Flag.
source: Conversely, cleavage-deficient DispCS failed to effectively promote Shh release into conditioned media when expressed alone or in combination with Scube2-Flag (Figure 4B, lanes 12–15 and black).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the Shh release assay shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 generated Furin-/- MEF clones were compromised in their ability to release ligand.
source: Whereas control MEFs released Shh into culture media, CRISPR/Cas9 generated Furin-/- MEF clones, which failed to effectively cleave V5DispHA, were compromised in their ability to release ligand (lanes 1–2 vs 3–4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the Shh release assay in Furin-/- cells shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The dDisp antibody detected two distinct bands, one migrating at the predicted molecular weight of ~150 kDa (dDisp150) and a second species with an approximate molecular weight of ~110 kDa (dDisp110).
source: The dDisp antibody detected two distinct bands, one migrating at the predicted molecular weight of ~150 kDa (dDisp150) and a second species with an approximate molecular weight of ~110 kDa (dDisp110).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the western blot shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A ~ 30 kDa V5 fragment was released from double-tagged V5dDispHA expressed in Cl8 cells.
source: Similar to what was observed for mouse Disp, a ~ 30 kDa V5 fragment was released from double-tagged V5dDispHA expressed in Cl8 cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the western blot shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both dDisp150 and dDisp110 bands were evident at equal levels in anti-Disp immunoprecipitates from wing imaginal disc lysate.
source: Both bands were evident at equal levels in anti-Disp immunoprecipitates, but not in IgG control immunoprecipitates, confirming that endogenous dDisp protein is processed in cultured fly cells and in vivo in wing imaginal discs.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunoprecipitation experiment shown in Figure 5A'.

claim: Deletion of the three putative cleavage sites ablated generation of dDisp110.
source: We therefore engineered an in frame deletion to remove sequence encompassing all three putative cleavage sites (Δ206–238), and tested for processing of the ΔCS mutant in Cl8 cells. Deletion of the three putative cleavage sites ablated generation of dDisp110 (Figure 5C lane 4 compared to 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the western blot shown in Figure 5C.

claim: dDisp110 of the wild type protein harbored complex N-linked glycans, indicative of post-ER localization.
source: Endo H and PNGase F sensitivity analysis revealed that like the mouse protein, dDisp110 of the wild type protein harbored complex N-linked glycans, indicative of post-ER localization (Figure 5C, lane 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the deglycosylation experiment shown in Figure 5C, with an inference about localization.

claim: Over-expression of wild-type dDispHA triggered obvious blistering of the adult wing.
source: Consistent with the established positive role of dDisp in Hh release (Burke et al., 1999), over-expression of wild-type dDispHA triggered obvious blistering of the adult wing (Figure 5E compared to D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the Drosophila wing phenotype analysis shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Over-expression of dDispΔCS triggered modest wing curling, but did not induce pronounced blistering.
source: By comparison, over-expression of dDispΔCS triggered modest wing curling, but did not induce pronounced blistering (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the Drosophila wing phenotype analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In control non-dDisp expressing salivary glands, Hh accumulated in large puncta on the basal surface of salivary gland cells.
source: In control non-dDisp expressing salivary glands, Hh accumulated in large puncta on the basal surface of salivary gland cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the salivary gland imaging shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Expression of wild-type V5dDispHA in salivary gland cells resulted in a mostly uniform membrane localization of HhGFP with distinct puncta evident throughout basolateral optical sections.
source: Expression of wild-type V5dDispHA in salivary gland cells resulted in a mostly uniform membrane localization of HhGFP with distinct puncta evident throughout basolateral optical sections (Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the salivary gland imaging shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Cells expressing V5dDispHAΔCS showed an overt increase in HhGFP puncta throughout basolateral optical sections with accumulation of large puncta at the basal surface.
source: Conversely, cells expressing V5dDispHAΔCS showed an overt increase in HhGFP puncta throughout basolateral optical sections with accumulation of large puncta at the basal surface that resembled puncta observed in the absence of V5dDispHA expression (Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the salivary gland imaging shown in Figure 5I.

claim: A ~ 480 kDa fraction consistent with the predicted molecular weight of the Disp trimer was evident for both wild type and cleavage deficient DispHA proteins.
source: A ~ 480 kDa fraction consistent with the predicted molecular weight of the Disp trimer was evident for both wild type and cleavage deficient DispHA proteins, indicating that blocking cleavage did not block trimer formation (Figure 6A, top).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the native gel electrophoresis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Larger molecular weight fractions (~750 kDa) were present at equal intensities for both wild type and CS proteins.
source: Moreover, larger molecular weight fractions (~750 kDa) were present at equal intensities for both wild type and CS proteins, suggesting cleavage disruption did not prevent murine Disp from forming higher order assemblies.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the native gel electrophoresis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Similar amounts of Shh co-immunoprecipitated on anti-HA beads with both WT and CS mutant DispHA proteins.
source: Similar amounts of Shh co-immunoprecipitated on anti-HA beads with both WT and CS mutant DispHA proteins (Figure 6B, lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the co-immunoprecipitation experiment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Colocalization between amino-V5 and carboxyl-HA, indicative of the unprocessed protein, was evident for wild type V5dDispHA in basal vesicles and along basolateral membranes.
source: Colocalization between amino-V5 (magenta) and carboxyl-HA (green), indicative of the unprocessed protein, was evident for wild type V5dDispHA in basal vesicles and along basolateral membranes (Figure 6C, white; F-Actin marks apical, blue).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the follicle cell imaging shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The released amino-terminal V5 fragment localized to apical and basolateral membrane and in vesicles throughout the cell.
source: The released amino-terminal V5 fragment, evidenced by V5 signal not colocalized with HA, localized to apical and basolateral membrane and in vesicles throughout the cell (Figure 6C, magenta).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the follicle cell imaging shown in Figure 6C.

claim: dDisp110HA depleted apically, enriching on basolateral membrane and in basally-localized vesicles.
source: Notably, dDisp110HA depleted apically, enriching on basolateral membrane and in basally-localized vesicles (Figure 6C, green), suggesting differential trafficking of the two dDisp domains post-cleavage.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the follicle cell imaging shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The cleavage site mutant showed pronounced accumulation on both apical and basolateral membranes, along with uniform vesicular distribution throughout the cell.
source: Visualization of cleavage-deficient V5dDispΔCSHA revealed a strikingly altered localization from that of the wild-type protein (Figure 6D). The cleavage site mutant showed pronounced accumulation on both apical and basolateral membranes, along with uniform vesicular distribution throughout the cell, suggestive of altered membrane trafficking upon cleavage loss.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the follicle cell imaging shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In cells expressing wild-type V5dDispHA, approximately 50% of the HA signal was colocalized with endogenous Rab5 signal.
source: In cells expressing wild-type V5dDispHA, approximately 50% of the HA signal was colocalized with endogenous Rab5 signal.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the colocalization experiment shown in Figure 6F-H.

claim: Cleavage site deletion lessened V5dDispHA-Rab5 colocalization, reducing the percent of HA signal colocalized with Rab5 signal to ~35%.
source: Cleavage site deletion lessened V5dDispHA-Rab5 colocalization, reducing the percent of HA signal colocalized with Rab5 signal to ~35% (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the colocalization experiment shown in Figure 6F-H.

claim: Disp is cleaved at a conserved processing site in its predicted first extracellular loop by the proprotein convertase Furin.
source: The study presented here improves understanding of Disp regulation by revealing an evolutionarily conserved cleavage event that influences the ability of Disp to deploy Hh family ligands from ligand-producing cells. We report that Disp is cleaved at a conserved processing site in its predicted first extracellular loop by the proprotein convertase Furin.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experiments including Edman sequencing, Furin inhibition, and Furin knockout experiments.

claim: Cleavage site mutation compromises Disp-mediated ligand deployment in vitro and in vivo.
source: Cleavage site mutation compromises Disp-mediated ligand deployment in vitro and in vivo, leading to reduced pathway activation in target cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by release assays (Figure 4B), reporter assays (Figure 4A), and in vivo phenotypes (Figure 5).

claim: This study is the first to provide mechanistic insight into a process promoting functional maturation of Disp for its role in ligand deployment.
source: As such, this study is the first to provide mechanistic insight into a process promoting functional maturation of Disp for its role in ligand deployment.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study stated in the discussion.

claim: Disp membrane trafficking is regulated in cleavage-dependent manner.
source: Because cleavage disruption altered full-length dDisp membrane localization in polarized epithelial cells to mimic what was observed for the processed 30 kDa V5 fragment, we hypothesize that like Nodal, Disp membrane trafficking is regulated in cleavage-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion based on the localization data from Figure 6.

claim: Cleavage occurs after basolateral targeting of unprocessed Disp.
source: The observed colocalization of amino- and carboxyl-terminal dDispWT epitope tags on basolateral membranes of Drosophila follicle cells suggests cleavage occurs after basolateral targeting of unprocessed Disp.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data from Figure 6C.

claim: Furin has been demonstrated to traffic basolaterally in polarized epithelial cells.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, Furin has been demonstrated to traffic basolaterally in polarized epithelial cells (Simmen et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to prior work.

claim: Cleavage-deficient Disp accumulated uniformly along apical and basolateral membranes of Drosophila follicle cells.
